lines: This shop's nightly warehouse rebuild runs long enough, and costs enough, that finance has started asking pointed questions about it.
The team switches that whole rebuild over to an incremental approach instead.
Weeks later, the warehouse's own order count comes up short against the source, because every cancelled order quietly never reappeared anywhere in that incremental extract.
Incremental loads genuinely have more than one way to go wrong, each in its own distinct fashion.
Only one of those failure modes produces a permanent, silent gap, rather than ordinary staleness that eventually catches back up on its own. Which one is it?
answer: A load that simply runs slower produces staleness: a count sitting behind, but one that eventually catches back up once the backlog clears.
A deleted row produces a gap that never closes by itself, because the extract was only ever built to pull rows that are changed or new, never to notice something quietly missing.

lines: One fact tracking each order line, another tracking a daily snapshot of inventory, surrounded by conformed customer, product, and date dimensions.
A decision card weighs three real alternatives side by side: a wide denormalised table, a Data Vault, and this dimensional model.
Each one gets priced specifically for this exact workload, not for some generic, average one.
A cancelled order's row simply vanishes at the source, with nothing left behind to mark that it ever happened.
The incremental extract, built only ever to pull rows that are changed or brand new, never once asks what's actually missing.
So that row sits in the warehouse forever, completely unless this design deliberately adds a clause that goes looking for it.
An order-line fact lands before its own customer dimension has even arrived yet.
Rather than drop that fact outright, or block the whole load waiting on it, it gets an inferred, placeholder dimension key instead.
That placeholder gets backfilled properly the moment the real dimension row actually shows up.
A customer's address change becomes a brand new row under the SCD policy that keeps its own full history intact.
A simple phone-number correction, by contrast, just overwrites the existing row under the policy that keeps no history of the old number at all.
Both of these merge by one stated unique key. Without that key, the load degrades quietly into pure append, and silently duplicates instead.
A genuinely small handful of derived marts serve this shop's own dominant queries. Not every mart somebody requests actually earns its own keep.
Revenue itself gets defined exactly once, inside one shared semantic layer.
That way it's never quietly recomputed slightly differently inside each separate mart that happens to need it.
A full refresh's own cost rises quite steeply as table size grows larger.
An incremental refresh's cost rises far more slowly, but it carries its own fixed overhead that a full refresh simply never pays.
Those two lines cross at one specific table size, computed directly from this shop's own real numbers.
Grain gets decided first, and only then does a model get chosen from three real alternatives.
A deleted row and a late-arriving dimension each get their own clearly named guard.

An SCD policy decides exactly what history gets kept; a unique key decides what merges cleanly instead of silently duplicating. And the full-versus-incremental crossover is one computed number, never simply a guess.
One more, to use this for real: a completely different table has been running incremental for well over a year now.
It sits well past the point where a full refresh would actually be cheaper, because nobody ever once recomputed that crossover as the table kept growing larger.
What's genuinely the right first move here?
answer: Incremental has failed is only ever a feeling, never an actual measurement of anything.
The crossover formula takes this exact table's own current size and change rate and states, quite directly, which side of that line it genuinely sits on right now.
That side may not even match whatever side the original symptom seemed to suggest.
